/ SPERRY HAMPTONS · SERVICE DESIGN & INTERNAL TOOLS

Designing for the Next Exit

Role

For a season I was the operator and acting product lead at Sperry Hamptons, an event tent company on Long Island that a close friend had just bought with an SBA loan.

I took the role to see the entrepreneurship-through-acquisition trend up close: whether buying a small business is a realistic path, and where modern tools could actually help one.

The owner's long-term goal is a business that keeps its value without its longest-serving people. My job was to find where the business ran on memory and paper, and replace that with systems the team would actually use.

The Problem

Sperry had been profitable for twenty years. A crew of six, most with five to ten years on the job, ran installs with little oversight. A sales manager brought in the work and one admin handled permits.

The business worked because those people carried it. Each job was spread across Excel, QuickBooks, AutoCAD, Gmail, Goodshuffle and paper, and the only thing connecting them was what the staff knew. Performance could be checked, but only by pulling numbers out of QuickBooks and rebuilding them in spreadsheets. For the team, that meant rework. For a future buyer, it meant risk.

Research

I worked inside the parts of the business I was designing for: back-office admin, sales, and site planning. Doing that work day to day showed me where information dropped between teams, which interviews alone would have missed.

I also sat in on the accounting calls. The owner, with a fractional CFO handling the accounting and filling gaps, was restructuring the financial statements so they showed how the business was actually performing, and which data points were too thin to trust. Learning to read the business from those spreadsheets told me what the systems needed to capture.

How a Job Moves

I mapped every job as a service blueprint: ten steps across three teams, from the first inquiry to unloading at the warehouse, with the tools each step runs on.

How a job ran when I arrived. What changed is further down.

The blueprint made the core problem visible. The job is the central object in the business, and nothing owns it. The same details get typed into the intake form, the invoice, the permit, the calendar and the pack list, and across 200 jobs a season there's no single place to see a job's status, cost or history.

What I Bought, Built and Scoped

— 01

Bought: payroll on Gusto

Labor came first. Every job touches it, hours were handwritten and re-keyed each pay cycle, and mistakes carried compliance risk. Payroll software already solves this well, so building was never on the table. Hours also stayed in Excel, giving payroll two systems of record. The design work was adoption: getting a crew used to paper timesheets to trust a digital clock.

— 02

Built: a site plan tool in Replit

Site plans were the slowest step in sales. Each one started as a scaled Google Maps screenshot with AutoCAD tent templates on top, then went through two or three rounds of revisions. Nothing off the shelf handled venue maps, tent layouts and client changes together, so I built a tool in Replit. Plans got faster to draw and easier to revise. With 60% of jobs at repeat venues, a saved plan is also a head start on next year's quote.

— 03

Scoped: agreements in DocuSign

Client and vendor agreements were printed, signed and filed by hand. I scoped DocuSign so every agreement is searchable and tied to its job. It's planned, not yet live.

Four Functions, One Test

By the end of the season I was evaluating the business as four functions, each against the same test: can a new owner see how it's performing without rebuilding it in a spreadsheet?

QuickBooks and a fractional CFO keep the books. What they lack is job-level labor and inventory data.

None of the four fully passes yet, and the reason is the same each time. The data exists in QuickBooks and Excel, but it isn't connected to the job it came from, so every answer takes manual work. The next thing to build is the job record itself: created at inquiry, then added to by each team instead of retyped. Lead source, labor, inventory and margin all hang off that one record, which is what makes the numbers checkable and the business transferable.

The second opportunity is crew knowledge. Installs depended on a core crew with five to ten years on the job, and the SOPs that existed sat in folders split between the office and the warehouse. An internal onboarding platform, with short video tutorials for each step of an install, would give new crew and contract labor a way to learn the work without relying on whoever was available to show them. It also turns that experience into something the business owns.

What I Took From It

I went in with two questions. Is buying a small business a realistic path? And where can modern tools make a real difference in one?

The first answer is yes, but it depends less on the deal than on people. A smooth transition needs a good relationship with the seller, and the new owner has to win the trust of a staff that has run the business for years.

The second answer surprised me. I expected the opportunity to be saving hours. It turned out to be capturing a few things at the level of the job that the business couldn't easily see:

Bookings by lead source
Shows which of ads, SEO, magazines, venues and referrals are worth paying for.
Margin per event
With fixed pricing, shows which job types and venues actually pay off. It's also what buyers and lenders look at to value the business.
Tent and crew capacity
With half or more of jobs booked mid-season, shows whether there's room to say yes to the next booking before it turns into a scramble.
Repeat venues
At 60% of jobs, recurring revenue a buyer can count on, and saved site plans that make each quote faster.

All four come from the same place, the job record. Getting that right does more for a small business than any single new tool, because it makes the business readable to its owner today and to whoever buys it next.

What I'd Do Differently

I'd start with a sandbox. Designing new workflows was the easy part. Testing them without disrupting a business in the middle of its season was much harder. Next time I'd make a safe place to run new workflows against past jobs first, before anything touched live bookings.

I'd also go deeper on AI automation. The stack was a handful of tools held together by people retyping the same job, and I'd spend more time finding which automated workflows could collapse it into fewer tools, designed so the same setup could carry over to other service businesses.

/ BETMGM · DESIGN SYSTEM

One system, 40+ brands

Role

I co-architected Dice, the design system BetMGM and Entain share across 40+ brands. I worked on the token structure, the component library and the rules for how teams adopt it and add to it.

Context

BetMGM is a joint venture between MGM Resorts and Entain, and Entain's platform runs more than 40 betting brands. After years of acquisitions the frontend was a patchwork, and a change in one place could break something somewhere else. When we redesigned BetMGM, teams kept rebuilding components that already existed, and the same bugs came back release after release.

Design Problems

— 01

The redesign had nothing to build on

We had a new design direction, but every team that tried to build it ran into the same inconsistent foundation. That's why we started the design system.

— 02

40+ brands, one foundation

It had to work for more than 40 brands, each with its own look, markets and product rules, and still be small enough for one team to maintain.

Key Design Decisions

— 01

Brands change values, not components

We used three layers of tokens. Reference tokens hold raw values like color, spacing and type. Semantic tokens give those values a job, like primary or caution. Component tokens apply them to specific UI. To re-theme, a brand swaps its reference tokens and leaves the components alone.

Brands gave up some control in return. Contrast and interaction behavior lived in the components, so we got accessibility right once instead of 40 times. It also meant agreeing on a naming system, so every token says where it applies and what it does.

Our token naming model, and how we decided what to call a new token.

— 02

One codebase with room for each team

Dice lived in one repository: a core library, plus folders for Sports, Casino and Player Experience, so each team could keep its own components on the same versioned code.

At first the design system team owned every change, to keep quality up while the core took shape. The plan was to open contributions to product teams later, using Brad Frost's snowflake model.

The button component in Storybook. This was an early MVP build, made to prove the concept before the full library.

— 03

Getting teams to use it

Each component went through four phases: investigation, design, development and product integration. Design, product, business and the squads each had a set point to weigh in, so a component reached product teams already agreed on.

Who was involved at each phase of a component, and the meetings that moved it along.

Teams were spread over five time zones, so we also ran workshops in Vienna, held weekly check-ins with regional teams and staffed a support channel.

Outcomes

Auditing buttons in a single product for a single brand turned up 108 code classes the Dice button could replace.

Product teams started planning component adoption into their sprints. BetMGM's CEO and Entain's chief product officer both called out the work for the time it would save across the business.

Dice was also a finalist for the Best Collaboration Award from Zeroheight.

What I'd Do Differently

I'd open up contributions sooner, even in a basic form. Keeping every change with the core team protected quality early on, but once adoption picked up, every new pattern had to wait on us.

/ BETMGM · KIOSK

Designed the self-service betting kiosk experience and its companion mobile flow, bringing sportsbook UI into physical retail spaces.

Search in one placeTeam logos for faster scanningBet slip always in view
/ BETMGM · PRODUCT STRATEGY

Unifying a $1.3B Sportsbook

Role

I led design for BetMGM's three core journeys, onboarding, discovery and bet placement, across mobile, web and kiosk, on a team of seven. On onboarding and discovery I worked with a designer who ran research and usability testing. As each journey became its own workstream, I helped set up the team and hire the designers who took them over.

Context

BetMGM made about $1.3B in net revenue across 23 markets, but it had grown fast and through acquisitions. Sports, Casino and Player Experience felt like three separate products, each with its own look, navigation and patterns.

Design Problems

— 01

Placing a bet was hard to find

The bet slip sat behind a tab. Navigation worked differently from section to section, and search showed up in several places. Users had to relearn the app as they moved around it.

— 02

Each platform did things its own way

Mobile, web and kiosk had drifted apart, so what users learned on one didn't carry over to the others.

— 03

Screens were cluttered

Inconsistent type, color, icons and hierarchy made screens hard to scan.

We wanted to get people from opening the app to placing a bet faster, in a live and regulated product, without breaking what existing users already knew.

Key Design Decisions

— 01

Keeping the bet slip in view

The bet slip was one of five tabs in the bottom navigation. I added a bet bar above the navigation that showed live bet status and opened the slip. Then I rebuilt the slip as a bottom sheet holding both open selections and placed bets, so users could bet without leaving the screen they were on.

The bet slip went from a tab to a bar above the navigation.

Bet slip and My Bets went from two pages to one bottom sheet.

Quickbet let users place a single or multi bet straight from the bar. Same-game parlay, which competitors already had, used our existing parlay patterns, so there was nothing new to learn. I also designed the error and confirmation states from placing a bet through settlement, so users always knew where their bet stood.

— 02

One navigation for the whole app

Sports and Casino each had their own bottom navigation, and search moved around depending on the section. We combined the navigation into one bar, put search in one place at the top, and switched filtering to pills for league, sport and market.

Separate Sports and Casino navigation, combined into one bar.

— 03

Easier-to-scan event lists

We reduced clutter and moved live events, main markets and key actions higher on the screen. Team logos, a consistent icon set and standard event layouts made long lists of games quicker to read.

Team logos and a tighter layout, closer to the sports apps people already used.

— 04

Same patterns on every platform

Navigation, filters and the bet slip worked the same way on mobile, web and kiosk, sized for each screen. Someone who'd used the app on their phone could walk up to a kiosk and already know how to bet.

The retail kiosk for sports and horse racing, with the same filters, layout and bet slip as mobile.

— 05

Shorter, clearer sign-up

Sign-up and identity checks were long, gave no sense of progress, and only showed errors after you submitted. With my research partner running usability tests, I added a progress indicator, moved error messages to each field as you type, and cut the flow from seven screens to five while meeting every regulatory requirement.

Errors moved from one banner after submitting to each field as you type.

Outcomes

Registration completion reached 94% after the sign-up changes. Third-party usability testing after launch showed better NPS and feedback across the main journeys, and support calls dropped as more users switched to in-app chat.

The navigation, bet slip patterns and feedback states later became the starting point for Dice, the design system now used across Entain's 40+ brands.

Splitting the work into journeys early also gave each one a clear owner, which made it possible to hire designers into specific roles.

What I'd Do Differently

Our best numbers came from sign-up. Next time I'd measure time to first bet and bet slip drop-off before redesigning the slip, so the part I owned had its own before and after.

/ CIGNA · PRODUCT STRATEGY

Built Around the Org Chart, Not the Member

Role

I joined Cigna's Digital Team early in the myCigna redesign and worked on research, information architecture and early concepts, which shaped the direction for the rest of the redesign. I then designed navigation, Find Care, and cost and price transparency, to make it easier for members to find care and know what it would cost.

Context

Cigna is one of the largest health insurers in the U.S., with millions of members on employer, government and individual plans. In 2017 it bought Brighter, a consumer-focused dental and vision startup, and people from that team went on to lead Cigna's Digital Team.

Design Problems

myCigna was organized around Cigna's internal departments, not around how members use their health plan.

— 01

Navigation followed the org chart

Find Care and Claims made up half of all app usage, but because the app mirrored Cigna's internal structure, both were hard to get to.

— 02

Urgent tasks took too many taps

Members usually opened the app to do one specific thing: find a provider, check a claim, pull up an ID card. Each of those took more navigation than it should have.

— 03

It felt like paperwork

Dense layouts, inconsistent hierarchy and a clinical look made healthcare feel more complicated than it is.

A heuristic audit of every core section, scored on task completion, accessibility, design quality and information architecture, rated accessibility 2 to 4 out of 10 in almost every flow, including Dashboard, Claims and ID Cards.

Research

Across 81M sessions, usage was concentrated. Find Care and Claims made up half of all activity.

A week-in-the-life study explained why. Members didn't browse myCigna. They came with one task in mind and wanted to get it done.

Key Design Decisions

— 01

Organizing by stage of care

In a whiteboarding session with Product and UX, we mapped the moments when members actually deal with their care, instead of the departments that owned each feature. That gave us a four-stage information architecture, with Help available everywhere instead of as its own stage.

The information architecture from that session, with every feature placed under a stage of care.

It became the structure for the whole redesign, and product teams still use it to decide where new features go.

— 02

Putting urgent tasks one tap away

We sorted every feature into three tiers of need: basic, secondary and self-fulfillment. The tier decided where it went. Find Care became a main destination, and the digital ID card moved into the bottom navigation instead of sitting in a secondary menu.

The basic-needs tier lined up almost exactly with the most-used sections: ID Cards, Claims, Accounts and Find Care.

— 03

A calmer, clearer interface

We rebuilt the interface with clearer type, more space, a softer hierarchy, and color and illustration only where they helped.

Managing health care is stressful, so we focused on making the information easier to take in.

Outcomes

The app has been visually updated since to match Cigna's new brand, but the structure from this work is still in use, and the app has won multiple J.D. Power Digital Experience Awards.

The bigger change was how the product is organized: around the member's care instead of Cigna's departments. This work also set up the full myCigna redesign and the mobile app that followed.

What I'd Do Differently

Our audit rated accessibility 2 to 4 out of 10 in almost every flow, and our early work focused on structure instead. I'd make accessibility its own track from the start instead of counting on the visual refresh to fix it.
